summary: Specifies Babel, a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol that works well in both ordinary wired networks and wireless mesh networks. This version obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557.

eli5.summary: Babel lets routers tell each other the best way to reach places, and it avoids sending packets around in circles, even on shaky wireless links.

questions: what is the babel routing protocol
routing protocol for wireless mesh networks
how does babel avoid routing loops
what is the babel feasibility condition
subtitle: A distance-vector routing protocol that stays loop-free on both stable wired networks and shaky wireless meshes.

tldr.problem: Plain distance-vector protocols such as RIP can suffer routing loops and black-holes while they reconverge after a link fails, which is especially painful in unstable wireless networks.
tldr.mechanism: Babel runs Bellman-Ford but only accepts a route announcement when it can prove the route cannot cause a loop (the feasibility condition). Sequence numbers and explicit requests rescue routers that run out of feasible routes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8966 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557. Babel is insecure as defined, so the RFC recommends MAC authentication or DTLS.

today: RFC 8966 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What Babel Is For
sections.content:
Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol. It is designed to be robust and efficient in networks that use prefix-based routing and in flat "mesh" networks, in relatively stable wired networks and in highly dynamic wireless ones.

Unlike naive distance-vector protocols, it strongly limits how often and how long routing loops and black-holes occur while the network reconverges. After a mobility event it usually stays loop-free, quickly settles on a working but not necessarily optimal configuration, and then slowly converges to the optimal one over a time on the scale of minutes. The RFC states the guarantees precisely: with one originator per prefix there are no routing loops, and with several originators a transient loop may occur, disappearing in time proportional to the loop's diameter.

Nodes with different parameters still form associations, so a battery-powered mobile node can use longer timers than a mains-powered one. Babel is also a hybrid protocol: it can carry routes for IPv4 and IPv6 regardless of which protocol carries the Babel packets.

There are two stated limitations. Babel relies on periodic updates rather than a reliable transport, so in large stable networks it sends more traffic than protocols that only speak on change, and the RFC points to OSPF, IS-IS or EIGRP there. And without an optional algorithm it imposes a hold time on retracted prefixes, which can make it unsuitable where automatic prefix aggregation is used.
sections.eli5: Babel is a set of rules for road signs between towns. It keeps the signs from ever pointing in a circle, even when roads keep closing and opening.

sections.title: Costs, Metrics and Bellman-Ford
sections.content:
For each pair of neighbouring nodes Babel computes a cost for the link. The metric of a route is the sum of the costs along it. Each node periodically sends Hello messages to its neighbours, and an IHU ("I Heard You") message to every neighbour it has recently heard a Hello from. From these a node derives the cost of the link.

The core algorithm is Bellman-Ford, run in parallel for every destination. Each node keeps an estimated distance and a next hop, and periodically advertises its distance to its neighbours. A neighbour adopts the route if it is through its current next hop or if it is better than the current one. Triggered updates speed convergence after a major change, and alternate routes can be kept for instant failover.

The RFC shows why plain Bellman-Ford misbehaves. When a link fails, nodes may switch to each other's stale routes and keep raising their metrics until they reach "infinity", a value larger than any the protocol can carry.

Routing metrics are a local policy choice as long as two conditions hold: an infinite cost gives an infinite metric, and the metric function is strictly monotonic. The additive metric is the RECOMMENDED default.
sections.eli5: Each road between two towns gets a score for how bad it is, and a trip's score is all the road scores added up. Towns keep telling their neighbours the best score they know for each place.

sections.title: Feasibility and Sequenced Routes
sections.content:
Babel routers discard route announcements unless they can show that accepting them cannot cause a loop. This test is the feasibility condition. A router A remembers its feasibility distance, the smallest metric it has ever advertised for a destination. An update from a neighbour is feasible only if the metric it advertises is strictly smaller than that. The RFC says this is derived from EIGRP and is less restrictive than the simpler rule used by DSDV and AODV, so it keeps more usable alternate routes.

Feasibility can leave a router with no feasible route even though a working one exists, which the RFC calls spurious starvation. Babel borrows sequenced routes from DSDV. Each route carries a sequence number that is only incremented by the originating source. Together with the metric it forms a distance, and an update is feasible if its sequence number is newer, or equal with a strictly smaller metric. Sequence numbers are 16-bit values compared modulo 2^16.

Instead of waiting for the source to bump its number periodically, a starving node sends an explicit seqno request towards the source. The source increments its sequence number and broadcasts an update. Requests ignore the feasibility condition, so nodes perform duplicate detection to avoid forwarding loops. Route selection itself MUST NOT prefer a route just because of a higher sequence number, which would cause oscillation.

When several routers originate the same prefix, such as a default route, feasibility distances are kept per source, a pair of router-id and prefix. Babel then cannot guarantee loop freedom in general, but any loop is broken once the update has gone around it, and the routers involved will not join a loop for those sources again until the source table entries are garbage-collected.
sections.eli5: A town only believes a new sign if it is sure that sign cannot lead back to itself. If it gets stuck, it asks the source town to stamp a newer date on its news, and then everyone trusts it again.

sections.title: How a Babel Router Behaves
sections.content:
Every Babel speaker has a router-id, an arbitrary string of 8 octets assumed unique across the routing domain. Babel packets travel in UDP datagrams, over IPv6 or IPv4. Using IPv6 exclusively for control traffic is RECOMMENDED because running both doubles the neighbour discovery and link-quality traffic. Packets may go to a well-known link-local multicast address or to a unicast address, and the source address is always unicast (link-local on IPv6).

Neighbours are found with Hello messages, which carry a sequence number and an interval. Multicast Hellos serve for neighbour discovery. A node SHOULD send periodic Multicast Hellos unless neighbour discovery happens by other means. Hello history lets a node estimate reception quality. Bidirectional reachability is confirmed with IHUs, which carry the sender's reception cost and an interval. Once a node knows both directions, it computes link cost by local policy under three rules: the cost is strictly positive, it is infinite if no Hellos arrived recently, and infinite if the transmission cost is infinite.

Routers advertise their selected routes in Update messages, at least once every update interval, plus triggered updates after significant change. A retraction is an update with an infinite metric. Route selection must never pick a retracted or unfeasible route; beyond that, the RFC says a strategy SHOULD include hysteresis, switching only when another route has been consistently good for some time, to avoid oscillation.

Besides seqno requests, a route request asks for an update for a given prefix. A node answers with an update if it has a selected route or a retraction if it does not. A wildcard route request asks for a full route table dump, which SHOULD be rate-limited. A node that loses all feasible routes but still holds unfeasible ones MUST send a seqno request, and the default hop count in the RFC's example is 64.
sections.eli5: Neighbouring routers keep saying hello and checking they can hear each other. Then they swap news of the best roads, and if a router loses its way it politely asks the destination to confirm that it still exists.

sections.title: Packets, TLVs and Defaults
sections.content:
A Babel packet has a 4-octet header, a body of TLVs, and an optional trailer of TLVs. The header holds a Magic byte of 42, a Version byte of 2, and a 16-bit body length. Packets with a different first or second octet MUST be silently ignored. A TLV starts with a Type and a Length, and TLVs with an unknown type MUST be silently ignored, which keeps the protocol extensible. Integers are big-endian, and times are 16-bit values in centiseconds.

The TLV types defined here are Pad1 (0), PadN (1), Acknowledgment Request (2), Acknowledgment (3), Hello (4), IHU (5), Router-Id (6), Next Hop (7), Update (8), Route Request (9) and Seqno Request (10). Update TLVs carry a prefix, sequence number, metric and interval, and use compression state to keep encodings compact.

Appendix B gives RECOMMENDED defaults. The Multicast Hello interval is 4 seconds, the Update interval is 4 times that, the advertised IHU interval is 3 times it, and the request timeout starts at 2 seconds and doubles on each resend, up to three times. The source garbage-collection time is 3 minutes. The Hello interval matters most: an outage is detected within 1.5 to 3.5 Hello intervals.

IANA registered UDP port 6696, the IPv6 multicast group ff02::1:6 and the IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.111 for Babel.
sections.eli5: Every Babel message starts with a secret handshake number so routers can tell it is really Babel, followed by little labelled boxes of news that a router can skip if it does not understand the label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is blunt: as defined here, Babel is a completely insecure protocol. It trusts information received in plaintext UDP datagrams. An attacker on the local network can spoof packets to redirect traffic, send malformed packets to crash fragile implementations, or replay captured packets.

Over IPv6, packets are ignored unless they come from a link-local address. Routers do not forward link-local packets, so attacks are restricted to on-link attackers. No such protection exists over IPv4, which is one reason IPv6 is recommended.

The RFC RECOMMENDS protecting all Babel traffic with an application-layer cryptographic protocol. There are two: Babel over DTLS (RFC 8968) provides authentication, confidentiality and integrity, and MAC authentication (RFC 8967) appends a message authentication code and freshness information to each packet. Every implementation SHOULD implement Babel-MAC, which is preferred where symmetric keys suffice and routing information is not confidential.

The RFC also warns about privacy: what a mobile node announces is enough to determine its physical location with reasonable precision. Randomly chosen router-ids and addresses, changed often, mitigate this somewhat.
sections.eli5: Plain Babel believes whatever it hears, like a town that follows any sign someone nails up. Adding a secret signature to every message makes sure only trusted neighbours can put up signs.

sections.title: Compatibility With Earlier Versions
sections.content:
RFC 8966 is the successor to RFC 6126 and RFC 7557. The protocols are not entirely compatible, but the new one is designed to be deployed in existing RFC 6126 networks without a flag day.

Three optional features break compatibility with the old protocol: Unicast Hellos, unscheduled Hellos (those with an interval of zero), and mandatory sub-TLVs. An implementation that never sends Unicast or unscheduled Hellos and uses no extension relying on mandatory sub-TLVs is safe to deploy alongside RFC 6126 and RFC 7557 nodes.

Other changes do not affect interoperability: route acquisition conditions are relaxed, route selection should no longer use the sequence number, the packet trailer format is defined, and router-ids that are all zeros or all ones are forbidden.
sections.eli5: New Babel can share a network with old Babel as long as the new one avoids the few new tricks the old one does not understand.

fields.name: Magic
fields.desc: The value 42; packets with another first octet are silently ignored.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: The value 2; packets with another second octet are silently ignored.

fields.name: Body length
fields.desc: Octets in the packet body, excluding this header and the trailer.
